texts.text: The honeybee can visit up to five thousand flowers in a single day, flying from dawn to dusk to feed its colony.
A good cup of coffee starts with fresh beans, clean water and a grind that matches the brewing method you prefer.
The Pacific Ocean is so vast that it covers more surface area than all the continents of the Earth combined. Its deepest trench plunges nearly eleven kilometers below the waves.
To be, or not to be, that is the question, wrote Shakespeare, giving Hamlet the most famous line in all of theatre.

texts.source: Charles Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities
texts.text: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, wrote Dickens, opening his novel of London and Paris at the dawn of the French Revolution.
Anything one man can imagine, other men can make real, wrote Jules Verne, the father of science fiction and a tireless prophet of technology.
You will face many defeats in life, but never let yourself be defeated, wrote Maya Angelou in her letters and memoirs.
The secret of getting ahead is getting started, said Mark Twain; the secret of starting is breaking big tasks into small steps.
Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood, and two of those hearts stop beating whenever the animal swims to save energy.
The Great Wall of China stretches over thousands of miles of mountains, deserts and plains across the north of the country.

Touch typing means writing without looking at the keyboard. Each finger rests on a home row key and reaches only for the keys assigned to it. The method feels slow at first, but after a few weeks of daily practice, muscle memory takes over and speed climbs steadily. Accuracy always comes before speed. Most patient learners double their speed within a few months.

The printing press changed the world in a single generation. Books that once took months to copy by hand could suddenly be printed by the hundreds. Ideas spread faster than ever before, literacy rose, and the price of books fell. Many historians consider it the most important invention of the second millennium. Gutenberg himself died poor, unaware of what he had started.

Lighthouses have guided sailors for more than two thousand years. The Pharos of Alexandria, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world, stood over a hundred meters tall and burned fires visible for miles. Modern lighthouses use powerful electric lamps and precise lenses, but their mission remains exactly the same. Most of them are now automated, with no keeper on site.

Chess arrived in Europe from India through Persia more than a thousand years ago. Each piece moves according to simple rules, yet the number of possible games is greater than the number of atoms in the observable universe. Grandmasters train for decades to recognize patterns that beginners cannot even see. The strongest computers now defeat every human champion.

Sourdough bread requires nothing but flour, water, salt and time. The starter, a living culture of wild yeast and bacteria, must be fed every day like a pet. Bakers learn to read its smell and texture. The slow fermentation gives the bread its open crumb, deep flavor and a crust that crackles. Some bakeries keep the same starter alive for decades.

Running is one of the simplest sports: put on shoes, step outside, and go. Coaches advise beginners to start slowly, mixing walking and jogging, and to increase distance by no more than ten percent per week. Most injuries come from doing too much too soon. Consistency, not intensity, builds the runner. A short run repeated all year beats a heroic sprint in January.

The Amazon rainforest produces a significant share of the oxygen we breathe and hosts one in ten known species on Earth. Its rivers carry more water than the next seven largest rivers combined. Scientists estimate that millions of species living under its canopy have yet to be discovered and named. Protecting this forest means protecting ourselves.

Learning a language rests on three pillars: vocabulary, grammar and daily practice. Fifteen minutes every day beats three hours on Sunday. Mistakes are not failures but stepping stones, and linguists agree that speaking imperfectly always beats staying silent perfectly. Regularity turns effort into instinct. New words stick when they meet real sentences.

Tea is the most consumed drink in the world after water. Born in China, it conquered Japan, India and finally Europe over the centuries. Green, black or smoked, every tea asks for its own water temperature and steeping time. In Japan, the tea ceremony turns its preparation into a precise art. Each gesture there has been refined over centuries.

A colony of bees may hold fifty thousand workers in summer, all serving a single queen. To tell their sisters where nectar lies, foragers perform a figure-eight dance that encodes direction and distance. Without their pollination, a large share of the fruits and vegetables we eat would simply disappear. Protecting bees means protecting our own food supply.

The first bicycles had no pedals at all: riders pushed the ground with their feet. By the end of the nineteenth century, the chain drive and equal-sized wheels created the safety bicycle we know today. The bike gave millions of people, especially women, a new and revolutionary freedom of movement. It remains one of the most efficient machines ever built.

The Mediterranean earned its name from the Romans, who saw it as the sea in the middle of the lands. Almost enclosed, it renews its waters slowly and stays fragile. Its floor hosts vast meadows of seagrass that store carbon and shelter young fish, nurseries on which much of its marine life depends. Overfishing and warming waters now threaten this balance.

The transcontinental railroad stitched the United States together in the nineteenth century. Before it, crossing the country took months of dangerous travel by wagon; after it, the journey shrank to about a week. Thousands of workers, many of them immigrants from China and Ireland, blasted tunnels through granite mountains and laid track across deserts and plains. The two companies racing from opposite coasts finally met at Promontory Summit, Utah, where a golden spike marked the moment. The railroad transformed the economy: mail, goods and people suddenly moved at unprecedented speed, towns sprang up along the line, and the vast interior of the continent was opened to settlement. Few engineering projects have ever reshaped a nation so completely and so quickly.

Sleep remains one of biology's great mysteries. Every night, the brain cycles through deep slow-wave sleep and the strange phase called REM, when dreams appear and the body lies almost paralyzed. During deep sleep, the brain consolidates the memories gathered through the day and flushes out metabolic waste. Studies show that chronic sleep loss erodes memory, mood and immune defenses alike. Yet our nights keep getting shorter, nibbled away by glowing screens and irregular schedules. Specialists recommend fixed hours, a cool dark room and a screen-free buffer before bed. Sleeping enough is not a luxury or a sign of laziness; it is a biological need as fundamental as food, and no amount of coffee can fully replace it.

Volcanoes fascinate as much as they frighten. Beneath the crust, magma gathers in chambers until the pressure grows too great, and the eruption hurls ash, gas and rivers of lava into the sky. Some eruptions shaped history: when Vesuvius buried Pompeii under ash, it froze a Roman city in time and gave archaeologists an unmatched window into daily life two thousand years ago. Others quietly build new landscapes, raising entire islands from the sea. Volcanoes are not only destructive; their soils rank among the most fertile on Earth, their hot springs provide energy, and their chemistry teaches us about the planet's interior. Modern science watches their tremors and swelling slopes, but predicting the exact hour of an eruption remains beyond our reach.

Silk shaped the history of trade between East and West for more than a thousand years. Spun by a humble moth caterpillar whose cocoon unwinds into a single filament hundreds of meters long, silk was so precious in China that revealing its secrets was punishable by death. Caravans crossed the deserts and mountains of Central Asia to carry it to the Mediterranean, lending their name to the famous Silk Road. Along with fabrics traveled religions, technologies and languages. Centuries later, the city of Lyon became Europe's silk capital, and its weavers built looms of growing ingenuity. The story of silk shows how an almost weightless fiber could move merchants across continents, found fortunes, and bind together civilizations that would otherwise never have met.

The bonsai is the art of growing miniature trees in pots, guiding their growth over years and sometimes generations. Born in China and refined in Japan, it demands a rare blend of patience, technique and artistic sense. The practitioner prunes roots and branches, wires twigs to bend their line, and chooses the pot with as much care as the tree itself. Despite a common belief, a bonsai is not a special species: almost any tree can be miniaturized, from maple to pine. The goal is not merely to keep a tree small but to suggest, within a few dozen centimeters, the strength of an ancient giant sculpted by wind and time. A fine bonsai tells a story of nature that humans accompany and shape but never truly command.

Photosynthesis is the process by which plants turn sunlight into chemical energy. In the leaves, chlorophyll captures photons and uses their power to assemble carbon dioxide and water into sugars, releasing oxygen as a byproduct. This mechanism, which first appeared in primitive bacteria billions of years ago, literally built the atmosphere of our planet and made life as we know it possible. Without it there would be no forests, no harvests, no food chains at all. Researchers still dream of copying the process artificially to produce clean fuels, yet nature keeps a comfortable lead: no technology rivals the quiet efficiency of a single green leaf tilted toward the sun. Every breath you take is, in a very real sense, a gift from photosynthesis.

The Tour de France began in nineteen hundred and three as a stunt to sell newspapers. The early editions were almost unimaginably brutal: stages longer than four hundred kilometers, heavy bicycles without gears, unpaved mountain roads, and riders repairing their own machines in the dark of night. Over the decades the race grew into a global spectacle with mythical climbs like the Galibier and Mont Ventoux, its distinctive jerseys and its legends written in sweat. Every July, millions of spectators line the roads of France just to watch the peloton flash past for a few seconds. The Tour remains at once an extreme athletic ordeal and a popular festival, woven so deeply into French culture that villages compete for the honor of hosting a stage start.

Versailles began as a modest hunting lodge built by Louis the Thirteenth in a marshy valley west of Paris. His son, Louis the Fourteenth, chose to make it the dazzling symbol of absolute power. For decades, architects, painters and gardeners transformed the site: the Hall of Mirrors dazzled ambassadors, the formal gardens drew perfect perspectives, and the entire court lived by a minute etiquette regulated by the king himself. Holding one's rank at Versailles was an art of every instant. The palace became the political heart of France until the Revolution, and courts across Europe copied its model. Today millions of visitors walk its gilded halls and gravelled alleys, witnesses of an age when architecture itself was a language of power, written in stone, gold and glass.
London, the capital of England, sits on the river Thames. The city has been a major settlement for two thousand years, since the Romans founded Londinium.
Spring returns at last: the days grow longer, the cherry trees blossom, and the first swallows trace swift circles in the warm evening sky.
In 1969, humans walked on the Moon for the first time. The Apollo 11 mission carried three astronauts across 384,000 kilometers of empty space.

The marathon covers exactly 42.195 kilometers. The distance was set at the 1908 London Olympics, running from Windsor Castle to the stadium finish line. Since then, millions of runners have tested themselves against the mythic distance, from the streets of Boston to those of Tokyo. The world record now flirts with the two-hour mark, a barrier long thought unbreakable.

Mount Everest rises 8,849 meters above sea level, the highest point on Earth. Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first reached its summit on May 29, 1953. More than 6,000 climbers have followed since, yet the mountain stays deadly: above 8,000 meters, the human body slowly shuts down. Every spring, long lines of climbers form near the final ridge.

Electricity became indispensable in less than a century: lighting, heating, transport, communications... In the United States, about 60% of power still comes from fossil fuels, while nuclear, wind and solar gain ground every year. The challenge of the next decades is to produce more while emitting less CO2. The power grid itself will have to adapt.

Morse code, invented in the 1830s, assigns each letter a pattern of dots and dashes: the letter E is a single dot, and the famous SOS reads ... --- ... Telegraph operators and sailors used it for over a century, saving countless lives at sea. A few radio amateurs still practice it today, for nostalgia or sport. Ships no longer use it, but the signal endures.

On July 21, 1969, at 02:56 UTC, Neil Armstrong set foot on the Moon: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." Apollo 11 had launched 4 days earlier from Cape Canaveral, carrying 3 astronauts nearly 384,000 kilometers from Earth. Michael Collins remained in orbit while Armstrong and Aldrin descended to the Sea of Tranquility. They spent about 21 hours on the surface, planted a flag, collected 21.5 kg of rock samples, and lifted off to rejoin the command module. The Apollo program cost over $25 billion and employed as many as 400,000 people. Twelve men walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972; no one has returned since. NASA now plans to send astronauts back.

The Internet grew out of an American military project: ARPANET, switched on in 1969, linked just 4 universities. Its principle was revolutionary — split messages into packets, route them along different paths, and reassemble them on arrival. In 1983, the TCP/IP protocol became the network's common tongue. But it was Tim Berners-Lee who, in 1989 at CERN, invented the Web: URLs, HTTP and HTML, the 3 building blocks that opened the network to everyone. The first website, published in 1991, simply explained how to build a website. Thirty years later, more than 5 billion people are online, and global traffic is measured in hundreds of exabytes — billions of billions of bytes exchanged every single year.

The Nobel Prize, created by Alfred Nobel's will in 1895, honors each year work conferring "the greatest benefit to humankind" in 6 fields: physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, peace and economics. The inventor of dynamite, holder of 355 patents, perhaps wished to redeem his legacy. The first ceremony took place in 1901; Marie Curie remains the only person to win 2 prizes in 2 different sciences (physics in 1903, chemistry in 1911). Each laureate receives a gold medal, a diploma and about 11 million Swedish kronor. Nominations stay secret for 50 years: there is no way to know who was shortlisted, how often, or why giants like Tolstoy, Joyce or Gandhi were never chosen.
